title: Projects, business as usual and change
blurb: Tell a project from business as usual, and explain how projects bring about the change an organisation needs.
question: A city library service is installing self-service kiosks in all its branches and training staff to use them. Meanwhile, the branches keep lending books every day. Which of these is the project, which is business as usual, and how do they connect?

teach.body: Every organisation does two kinds of work. It runs today's operations, and it changes them so tomorrow is better. APM defines a project as a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to bring about change and to achieve planned objectives. In plain English: a one-off piece of work, with a start and an end, that moves the organisation from how things are to how they need to be. Everything else in this course builds on that idea.

teach.caption: Business as usual (BAU) is the organisation's steady state. Projects disturb that steady state on purpose.

teach.h: Projects create change; BAU absorbs it
teach.body: A project is never the end goal. It produces outputs (a new system, building or process), then hands them to BAU. Only when BAU starts using those outputs does the organisation actually change and the value begin to flow. That is why the two must be linked from the start: a project that builds something BAU cannot or will not use has spent money for nothing.

teach.h: How change moves through an organisation

steps.label: New BAU
steps.sub: Improved way of working, benefits flow

teach.caption: The project sits between two versions of BAU. Its job is to get the organisation safely from one to the other.

teach.h: Is it a project? Ask two questions

children.label: Project
children.sub: Manage with a life cycle, plan and sponsor

children.label: Business as usual
children.sub: Manage through line management and processes

teach.caption: Both tests must be passed. Repeating the same job many times fails 'unique'; work that never ends fails 'temporary'.

items.label: Kiosk support and paper orders: BAU

teach.caption: Northgate Library Service wants shorter queues. The kiosk work is unique, has an end date and a clear objective: a project. Lending books and running story time carry on as BAU throughout, and once the kiosks are live, looking after them joins BAU too.

head: Work
Type
Why
rows: Moving payroll to a new system

teach.text: Classic exam trap: 'it has a start and an end date, so it's a project'. Not enough. The work must also be UNIQUE. Building 50 identical houses to one design, or running a monthly report, can have dates yet still be routine. And a 'project' that never ends and just keeps tweaking has quietly become BAU.

teach.body: Projects are riskier than BAU because the work is new, so they need their own governance: a sponsor, a plan, decision points and a defined end. Treat a project like BAU and it drifts without control. Treat BAU like a project and you add cost and paperwork to routine work. In a linear life cycle the change usually reaches BAU in one handover at the end; in an iterative one, BAU receives it in increments as each release goes live.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define both: a project is a unique, transient endeavour to bring about change; BAU is ongoing, repeatable operations.
Differentiate on at least three points (purpose, duration, uniqueness, team, risk), giving the reason for each.
Explain the link: the project delivers outputs; BAU adopts them so the benefits are realised.
Apply it to the scenario in the question: name the project work and the BAU work.
Say why it matters: the right management approach and governance for each.
Project: a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to bring about change and achieve planned objectives.
BAU: the ongoing, repeatable operations that keep the organisation running.
A project needs BOTH tests: unique and temporary. Dates alone are not enough.
Projects create change; BAU absorbs it, and that is where benefits are realised.
Getting the classification right means the right governance for each kind of work.

summary: You can now define a project in APM terms, tell it apart from business as usual on purpose, duration, uniqueness, team and risk, and spot the trap of judging by dates alone. You can also explain how projects deliver change that BAU then absorbs, which is where the value is realised.

A.q: Which statement best describes a project in APM terms?
options: A repeatable process that keeps services running
A unique, transient endeavour that brings change
Any piece of work with a budget and a manager
A permanent team set up to improve operations
A.why: APM defines a project as a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to bring about change and to achieve planned objectives.

whyNot.0: A repeatable process that keeps services running describes business as usual.
whyNot.2: Plenty of BAU work has a budget and a manager. Uniqueness and a defined end are what make a project.
whyNot.3: Project teams are temporary; a permanent improvement team is part of the line organisation.

A.q: Which of the following is MOST likely to be business as usual?
options: Installing a new booking system at a clinic
Relocating a head office to a new building
Launching a first loyalty scheme for shoppers
Processing the weekly payroll for all staff
A.why: Weekly payroll is ongoing and repeated in the same way every cycle: that is business as usual.

whyNot.0: Installing a new system is a one-off change with an end point, so it is a project.
whyNot.1: A relocation is unique and temporary, so it is a project.
whyNot.2: Launching a first scheme creates something new; running it afterwards becomes BAU.

A.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between a project and business as usual?
options: The project creates change; BAU absorbs it
BAU designs the change; the project runs it
Both run forever side by side, unconnected
The project replaces BAU once it is finished
A.why: Projects deliver outputs that change the organisation; BAU adopts and sustains them, which is where benefits are realised.

whyNot.1: It is the other way round: the project delivers the change, and BAU operates the result.
whyNot.2: Projects are temporary, and they are closely linked to BAU through transition.
whyNot.3: BAU continues after the project, in its new, improved form. It is not replaced.

B.q: A bakery chain bakes the same loaf to the same recipe in identical batches. Each batch has a clear start and finish. Why is this NOT a project?
options: Each batch is far too short to need planning
It has no separate budget or named sponsor
The work is repeated, so it is not unique
Bread is a product, not a system or service
B.why: Having a start and finish is not enough. A project must also be unique, and identical batches are routine, repeatable work.

whyNot.0: Duration does not decide it; a short piece of unique change can still be a project.
whyNot.1: Budgets and sponsors are features of how work is governed, not the test of what a project is.
whyNot.3: Projects can deliver any kind of output, including physical products.

B.q:
Which TWO characteristics together distinguish a project from business as usual?
1) Temporary
2) Repetitive
3) Unique
4) Uses a budget
options: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
B.why: A project is unique and transient (temporary). Both must be true.

whyNot.1: Temporary is right, but BAU uses budgets too, so a budget does not distinguish a project.
whyNot.2: Unique is right, but repetitive work is a sign of BAU.
whyNot.3: Repetitive describes BAU, and both projects and BAU use budgets.

B.q: Northgate Library's kiosks are installed, staff are trained and the kiosks are in daily use. A technician now fixes faults whenever they occur. How should this fault-fixing be classified?
options: Still the project, as it supports its outputs
BAU, because it is ongoing operational support
A new project each time a kiosk breaks down
A programme, because it follows on from a project
B.why: Once outputs are handed over, keeping them working is ongoing, repeatable support: business as usual.

whyNot.0: The project ended at handover. Supporting the outputs afterwards is operational work.
whyNot.2: Routine repairs are repeatable, not unique, so they are not separate projects.
whyNot.3: A programme coordinates related projects and BAU to deliver strategic benefits; routine repairs are not one.

C.q: Why does it matter whether a piece of work is managed as a project or as business as usual?
options: It decides whether the work needs any budget
BAU work never needs managers or planning
Only projects may make use of specialist staff
It shapes the governance and management approach
C.why: Projects are new and riskier, so they need their own governance (sponsor, plan, decision points, defined end). Routine work is better run through BAU processes.

whyNot.0: Both projects and BAU have budgets.
whyNot.1: BAU is managed too, through line managers and established processes.
whyNot.2: Specialists work in both projects and BAU.

C.q: A hospital trust's 'patient app' project began six years ago. The team now fixes small bugs and adds minor tweaks every month, with no end date planned. What should the sponsor most appropriately do?
options: Extend the project end date by another year
Restart the project with a new business case
Close the project and hand the work to BAU
Keep it as a project so the team stays together
C.why: The work is now ongoing and routine, so it has become BAU. The project should be closed and the support handed to an operational owner.

whyNot.0: Extending the date does not fix the problem: the work itself is no longer unique or temporary.
whyNot.1: A new business case would be right for a genuinely new change, not for routine support.
whyNot.3: Keeping a team together is not a reason to treat routine work as a project.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a valid difference between projects and business as usual?
options: Projects aim at change; BAU aims at stability
Projects are governed; BAU has no governance
Projects are temporary; BAU work is ongoing
Projects are unique; BAU work is repeatable
C.why: BAU is governed too, through line management, policies and processes. Projects simply need their own, temporary governance on top.

whyNot.0: This is a true difference: projects change things; BAU keeps them running.
whyNot.2: This is a true difference: projects are transient; BAU continues.
whyNot.3: This is a true difference: uniqueness is one of the defining features of a project.

reteach.title: Opening a new restaurant
reteach.question: A chef opens her first restaurant: she finds a site, fits out the kitchen, hires staff and holds an opening night. After that, she serves dinner six nights a week. Which part is the project and which is business as usual?

blocks.body: Getting the restaurant open is the project. It happens once, it has a goal (open by a set date, within a set budget) and the builders and designers leave when it is done. Dinner service is business as usual: the same routine every night, run by a permanent team. The project's whole purpose is to hand a working restaurant over to that nightly routine.

steps.label: The idea
steps.sub: A gap in the local market

steps.label: Fit-out project
steps.sub: Site, kitchen, staff, menu: done once

blocks.text: Each dinner service has a start and an end time, but it is not a project: it is the same routine repeated. A one-off refit of the dining room next year would be a new project.

explain.body: Unique: it has not been done in exactly this way before. Transient: it has a defined start and end. Endeavour: a deliberate effort. To bring about change and achieve planned objectives: it exists to move the organisation somewhere specific.

letters.sub: Not a repeat of routine work

test.q: Which word in the APM definition of a project means it has a definite start and end?
options: Transient
Unique
Endeavour
Objectives
test.why: Transient means temporary: the project exists for a limited time, from start to close.

whyNot.1: Unique means the work has not been done in exactly this way before.
whyNot.2: Endeavour means a deliberate effort; it says nothing about duration.
whyNot.3: Objectives are what the project aims to achieve, not how long it lasts.

explain.body: BAU is the organisation's steady state: the ongoing, repeatable operations that serve customers day to day. It is run by permanent teams through established processes and line management. It is the home every project's outputs must go to.

test.q: Which is the BEST description of business as usual?
options: Short-term work to build a new capability
A group of related projects giving benefits
A one-off change with planned objectives
The ongoing, repeatable running of operations
test.why: BAU is the ongoing, repeatable operation of the organisation: its steady state.

whyNot.0: Short-term work to build something new describes a project.
whyNot.1: A group of related projects delivering benefits describes a programme.
whyNot.2: A one-off change with planned objectives is a project.

explain.body: A project's outputs are only the means. The organisation changes, and benefits begin, when BAU adopts and uses them. A kiosk in a box helps nobody; kiosks in daily use cut queues.

test.q: At which point does the value of a project usually start to be realised?
options: When the business case is first approved
When the project team is first assembled
When BAU begins using the project outputs
When the final supplier invoice is paid
test.why: Value comes from using the outputs. Benefits start to flow once BAU adopts them.

whyNot.0: Approval allows the project to start; nothing has changed yet.
whyNot.1: Forming a team is an early step and delivers no value on its own.
whyNot.3: Paying invoices is part of closing the project, not a source of benefit.

explain.body: In a linear life cycle, outputs usually reach BAU in one transition near the end. In an iterative life cycle, BAU receives working increments after each release, so change, and some benefits, arrive earlier and in smaller steps.

test.q: In an iterative project, how does change typically reach business as usual?
options: All at once, after the final iteration ends
In increments, released after iterations
Only after a programme has been set up
It doesn't: iterative work stays in projects
test.why: Iterative projects release working increments into use, so BAU absorbs the change step by step.

whyNot.0: A single handover at the end is typical of a linear life cycle.
whyNot.2: Iterative projects do not need a programme in order to hand over increments.
whyNot.3: Every project's outputs must reach BAU, or no benefits are realised.
